questions.title: What is the scope of appellate jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 for reviewing BIA asylum decisions?
questions.question_body: In *Jimenez v. Bondi* the Tenth Circuit cites 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(1) and (b)(9) as giving it jurisdiction to review the Board’s denial of asylum. I’m confused about how a "final order of removal" includes a discretionary grant of asylum, which is normally within the Attorney General’s sole discretion. Does every denial of asylum constitute a final order that can be appealed? And how does the court decide whether it should look at only the administrative record versus also consulting the immigration judge’s explanation?

questions.title: When do threats or psychological harm rise to the level of ‘past persecution’ under INA § 1101(a)(42)(A)?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that "threats alone are insufficient" and that emotional distress from threats does not constitute persecution, citing *Karki v. Holder* and others. However, I have seen other cases where sustained threats were considered sufficient for past persecution. What threshold must be met for conduct to qualify as past persecution? Specifically, how do courts evaluate cumulative threats, physical harm, and lasting psychological injury?

questions.title: How must an applicant prove that political opinion is a ‘central reason’ for persecutor’s motive?
questions.question_body: The court held that Jimenez’s political affiliation was "tangential" because the primary motive for the attacks was his involvement in a property dispute with Don Rafa. What evidence is required to show that political opinion was at least one central reason for persecution? In mixed‑motive cases, how do courts allocate weight among multiple motives, and what distinguishes a "central" reason from an incidental one?

questions.title: Why does failure to report past persecution to police hurt an applicant’s ‘unable or unwilling’ government protection claim?
questions.question_body: In *Jimenez v. Bondi* the majority notes that petitioners made little effort to seek help from Colombian authorities and therefore cannot demonstrate that the government was unable or unwilling to protect them. How critical is an official police report in this analysis? What kinds of circumstances make a lack of reporting harmless (e.g., futility or danger), and how have other circuits applied this standard?

questions.title: What criteria do courts use to assess safe internal relocation for asylum seekers?
questions.question_body: The Tenth Circuit concluded petitioners could safely relocate within Colombia because they spent three weeks with family in the countryside and their relatives remain unharmed. I’m unclear on what factual findings satisfy the "reasonable opportunity" test for internal relocation. How do courts evaluate factors such as family ties, prior safe residence, local conditions, and "fundamental changes" in circumstances?

questions.title: How does the burden of proof differ between asylum and withholding of removal claims?
questions.question_body: "Jimenez v. Bondi" says that because petitioners failed on their asylum claim they also fail on withholding of removal since it requires a higher standard. Can someone explain what evidentiary standards apply to each form of relief under INA § 1158(b) and § 115(b)(2)? Does withholding require proof of past persecution only, or also a higher likelihood threshold for future persecution?

questions.title: Why did the Tenth Circuit not address petitioners’ due‑process claim against the immigration judge or their CAT claim?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that petitioners raised due‑process arguments regarding counsel rights and also sought protection under the Convention Against Torture, yet these issues were not decided because they were not appealed. Does appellate review under § 1252 allow a court to ignore unraised issues entirely, or could those claims still be raised on remand? What procedural rules govern which arguments are preserved for appellate consideration?
